lines.text: Why do LED lights use so little electricity?
These two bulbs give the same light: eight hundred lumens. One burns sixty watts. The other, eight.
The real question isn't how the LED saves energy. It's where the other fifty-two watts went.
They went into heat. And that wasn't a flaw. It was the method.
To make a filament glow, you heat it white-hot, past two thousand degrees.
At that temperature, almost everything it gives off is invisible infrared. Less than five percent was ever light.
An LED doesn't make light by heating anything.
Inside, there's an energy step. When an electron drops down it, it lets go of a photon.
The height of the step sets the color.
There's no wasted infrared, because nothing is hot enough to give it off. And that changes the math.
The old bulb gave about fifteen lumens per watt. A good LED tops a hundred.
For every hundred watts, around thirty come out as light, instead of five.
An LED gets warm too, but from losses, not from the method.
So an LED isn't a bulb that uses less.
The bulb was never really a lamp. It was a heater that happened to glow.
